title: Anthropic safety lead Joe Benton quits, joins METR with an extinction warning
subtitle: The Scalable Oversight manager's departure — the second Anthropic safety exit in three days — argues that the race to superintelligence is now underfunding the work that would let anyone stop it.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Joe Benton, until recently the manager of Anthropic's Scalable Oversight team, announced on September 11 that he had left the company two weeks earlier and is joining METR — the Berkeley-based Model Evaluation and Threat Research nonprofit — to run independent risk assessments on frontier systems. In statements to Business Standard and other outlets Benton framed the move plainly: frontier labs are racing to build systems that can recursively improve themselves toward what he called superintelligence, and the competitive dynamics of that race are chronically underfunding the safety work that would make an intelligence explosion recoverable. He said humanity 'may not survive' if that pattern holds. His exit follows Jacob Coxon's resignation from Anthropic on September 9 with a similar warning.

The specific worry Benton names is not that any single model is dangerous today — it is that the compounding pressure of a multi-lab race pushes every player to spend just enough on safety to avoid a public incident and not enough to actually catch an unsafe capability before it ships. Scalable Oversight, the team he ran, is the subfield that tries to invent evaluation techniques that keep working as models get smarter than the humans grading them. His argument is that a single company cannot honestly grade its own model against that bar while it is also trying to win the next benchmark, which is why he is moving to METR — an outside evaluator that already holds the eight-week investigation mandate Anthropic granted after its September 9 CTF disclosure.

Read against the last month of AI news, this is not an isolated protest resignation. It follows the Anthropic CTF-incident disclosures, the OpenAI dsewiki agent-hijack disclosure, the Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki 'alien mind' remarks about GPT-6 Astra, and the growing pattern of frontier labs handing evaluation transcripts to outside bodies for the first time. The people who built the scalable-oversight programs inside those labs are, one by one, saying the programs cannot do the job from inside — and moving to institutions that can. METR gaining a former Anthropic team lead in the same month it took the four-incident mandate is a meaningful staffing shift for the independent-evaluation ecosystem.

Takeaway for learners: how a field talks about its own safety is a leading indicator, and departure statements from people who managed the work are the loudest form of that talk. If you are choosing where to build a career in AI, watch which institutions are hiring the researchers who are leaving frontier labs — right now that is METR, the UK AI Security Institute, and a small number of academic centers. The internal safety team of a frontier lab and an external evaluator are increasingly different jobs, and the second one is where the current wave of experienced people is going.
